reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: Shear-lag correctly shows that a more compliant interlayer lowers the peak edge shear, but peel stresses of the same order are ignored and a sprayed gradient will be less ideal than the exponential profile (whose softest 12 um dominate), so about 35 % lower peak delamination stress. Delamination from damage edges is a secondary failure mode of foul-release coatings; cuts and tears in the topcoat dominate, so the effect on time-averaged friction is a few tenths of a percent.
key_assumption_issues: Interlayer stiffness of the graded interphase (2.6e10 Pa/m) from an idealised exponential profile; its value sets the gain
Baseline tie coat shear modulus 6.7 MPa is an assumption; softer tie coats would reduce the difference
Peel (normal) edge stresses and large membrane strain (0.33) neglected
killer_risks: Main damage mode (cutting and tearing of the soft topcoat) is unaffected
Soft zone of the interphase becomes the new weak plane (cohesive failure)
Reproducible gradient spraying on a hull in dock conditions is uncertain

reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: Switching only during idle periods removes a share of unconsolidated slime; with ageing of the molecular LCST layer and uncertain per-switch release of marine diatoms, about 12 % less retained slime is realistic, worth about half a percent of time-averaged friction. A conventional brush-grooming robot on the baseline would likely achieve as much.
key_assumption_issues: Release probability 0.5 per switch and consolidation time 1 day are assumptions
Linear flux model; idle-period consolidation effect only noted
The fair competitor (baseline plus a brush-grooming robot) is not simulated
killer_risks: The robot, not the coating, carries the benefit; proactive brush grooming of the baseline gives similar slime control at lower complexity
Molecular LCST brush ages or is masked within months
Robot logistics and cost on large merchant ships

reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: The 95 % is just the input friction ratio; in the field sand, biofilm and wear of the nm layer raise the friction coefficient to perhaps 0.1-0.25 over the service interval, so about 40 % lower contact shear on average. Without grooming the coating alone gives little objective benefit (about 0.5 % through less contact damage); the larger potential requires an operational grooming regime.
key_assumption_issues: Gain equals the assumed friction ratio 0.02/0.4; no tribology is simulated
Lab friction coefficients of clean hydration-lubricated surfaces used for sea conditions
The nm lubricating layer is assumed to persist under the contacts it lubricates
killer_risks: Abrasion of the PC layer by the brushes and fenders within months
Masking by biofilm and conditioning films removes the hydration lubrication
Squeeze-out of the hydration layer under fender pressures above ~1 MPa
